concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

concepts.name: mixed reality
concepts.definition: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

defining_facts.text: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
There is no agreement among practitioners and in the literature on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR).

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

defining_facts.text: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.

Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.
In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.
Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

concepts.name: Sensorama
concepts.definition: In 1962, Morton Heilig introduced Sensorama, which can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: In 1962, Morton Heilig introduced Sensorama, which can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality.

Sensorama was publicized as having 3D, wide vision, motion, color, stereo sound, smell, wind, and vibrations (haptics), and it stimulated all sensory organs by letting a user feel pre-recorded vibrations, sounds, smells, and wind.

concepts.name: force feedback device
concepts.definition: In 1967, Fred Brooks at the University of North Carolina developed a haptic feedback system that used a force feedback device to let a user feel, through touch, objects shown on a screen while manipulating them.

defining_facts.text: In 1967, Fred Brooks at the University of North Carolina developed a haptic feedback system that used a force feedback device to let a user feel, through touch, objects shown on a screen while manipulating them.

Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

concepts.name: pose
concepts.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

defining_facts.text: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.
Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.
The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors.

In outside looking in infrared tracking, cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object detect targets attached to the object and use them to determine the object's pose and position.
In inside looking out infrared tracking, the camera is mounted with the user and detects external targets, from which it estimates poses.

concepts.name: Microsoft HoloLens
concepts.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

defining_facts.text: The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities.

Virtual reality (VR) headsets may not include some advanced features of augmented reality (AR) headsets and typically have fewer components than an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens, because VR does not need to provide a real-world view.
The Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.

Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, and the device is equipped with detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

concepts.name: smell
concepts.definition: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

defining_facts.text: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

There is much less research on integrating smell and taste into extended reality (XR) systems than on visual, auditory, and touch senses, and fewer electronic devices have been made or are being made to provide stimuli to the nose and tongue, the body organs responsible for smell and taste.

Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama.

concepts.name: receptor
concepts.definition: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

defining_facts.text: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.
For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ.
Different types of receptors include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis.
Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.
The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense.

concepts.name: chemoreceptor
concepts.definition: Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter, on the tongue for taste and in the nasal passage for smell.

defining_facts.text: Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter, on the tongue for taste and in the nasal passage for smell.

Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

concepts.name: neuron
concepts.definition: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.

defining_facts.text: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
A neuron has a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, branches of the axon, and axon terminals.

The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

A neuron can aggregate information from other neurons, including information that has already been aggregated by other neurons, through the network of dendrites, and the processing that takes place in the nucleus or cell body is transmitted to one or more other neurons through axons.

For an interconnection between neurons, an axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next neuron, but the axon and dendrite are not physically connected; communication occurs across a gap called the synapse, through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.
In the human brain, each neuron has on average about 7,000 synaptic connections to other neurons, which results in about 10^15 edges in the brain's neuron-interconnection graph.

concepts.name: proprioception
concepts.definition: Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.

defining_facts.text: Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.
The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

Proprioception, called the sixth sense, is the conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable human body part, such as legs, arms, fingers, tongue, mouth, and lips, relative to other body parts.
The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis.

The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

never_defined.name: virtual world
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: virtual environment
never_defined.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

never_defined.name: body suit
never_defined.definition: Fully immersive virtual reality (VR) systems, such as dedicated virtual shooting game zones, use many devices such as helmets, gloves, body connectors with sense detectors, and body suits, so users view the virtual environment through a helmet or head-mounted display and their actual movements, such as running, jumping, crouching, shooting, and throwing, their reactions, and even a blink of an eye are detected and translated into actions in the virtual world while the user cannot sense anything in the real world.

never_defined.name: haptic device
never_defined.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.
